answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine Shakespeare, and easy to pin down: the lines belong to Duke Senior in As You Like It, act 2, scene 1, addressing his fellow exiles in the Forest of Arden. The play was never printed in quarto — it first appeared in the 1623 First Folio, which reads “Findes tongues in trees, bookes in the running brookes, / Sermons in stones, and good in euery thing.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Act 2, scene 1 — Duke Senior, to his fellow exiles in the Forest of Arden
First Folio, 1623 — the play was never published in quarto
“Findes tongues in trees, bookes in the running brookes, / Sermons in stones, and good in euery thing.”

source.excerpt:
Sweet are the uses of adversity,
Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous,
Wears yet a precious jewel in his head.
And this our life, exempt from public haunt,
Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks,
Sermons in stones, and good in every thing.
trail: The Folger Shakespeare edition of act 2, scene 1 ↗ prints the three lines consecutively inside Duke Senior's opening speech, immediately after “Sweet are the uses of adversity.”

The 1623 First Folio text at Internet Shakespeare Editions ↗ gives the original spelling: “And this our life exempt from publike haunt, / Findes tongues in trees, bookes in the running brookes, / Sermons in stones, and good in euery thing.”
The same edition's textual introduction ↗ states that the play “was not published in quarto at all” and first appeared in print in the Folio of 1623, which is “the sole authority” for its text.
Wikiquote's sourced entry for the play ↗ lists the passage under Act II, scene i and assigns it to Duke Senior, matching the editions above.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text; the 1623 Folio prints “euery thing” as two words, and modern editions such as the Folger's and Project Gutenberg's set it as “everything.”

source.rightsNote: As You Like It was first printed in the 1623 First Folio, more than three centuries before the 1931 US copyright threshold, so both the Folio wording and long-standing modern-spelling texts of it — including Project Gutenberg's edition ↗ — are in the public domain. Individual modern annotated editions may carry their own editorial copyright, but the sentence quoted here is Shakespeare's own text.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Shakespeare wrote roughly three dozen plays and 154 sonnets while working as an actor and shareholder in the company that became the King's Men. As You Like It is one of the pastoral comedies of his middle period, and about half his plays — this one included — survive only because his colleagues gathered them into the 1623 First Folio seven years after his death. He is also the single most magnetic name in quotation culture, which makes the lines that are demonstrably his worth marking clearly.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with it
misattribution.intro: The poet is right and the play is right. What drifts is the wording, the punctuation, and the fact that a character — not Shakespeare — is doing the talking.

items.why: A clipped version circulates that drops “And this our life, exempt from public haunt” and turns “Finds” into “Find,” which breaks the grammar: Goodreads carries it as “Find tongues in trees, books in the running brooks…” ↗. In the play it is “this our life” that finds them.
Quote aggregators insert a comma after “this” and name no play at all — BrainyQuote prints “And this, our life, exempt from public haunt…” with no work cited ↗.

The lines are Duke Senior's, spoken to his fellow exiles in the Forest of Arden as an argument that banishment is preferable to court — see the scene in the Folger edition ↗. Quoting it as Shakespeare's personal creed strips the irony out of it.

misattribution.truthLine: The 1623 First Folio — the only early printing of the play — reads “And this our life exempt from publike haunt, / Findes tongues in trees, bookes in the running brookes, / Sermons in stones, and good in euery thing” (Internet Shakespeare Editions, Folio 1 ↗).

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: The speaker is not a nature poet on a country walk. Duke Senior has been deposed by his own brother and is living rough in the Forest of Arden, and this speech is him talking himself into liking it — three lines earlier he says “Sweet are the uses of adversity.” The famous sentence is the punchline of an argument that exile beats the court, delivered by a man with every reason to need the argument to be true.

The thought itself has an older pedigree: Bernard of Clairvaux wrote in a twelfth-century letter that “Trees and stones will teach you what you cannot learn from masters” ↗. Shakespeare's version is the one that stuck, largely because of the sound of it — books/brooks, sermons/stones — which is also why it survives being ripped out of the play and pasted onto calendars.
detailsBody: The First Folio sets the passage as “And this our life exempt from publike haunt, / Findes tongues in trees, bookes in the running brookes, / Sermons in stones, and good in euery thing.” Everything modern editors do to it is spelling and punctuation; the words are the Folio's.
Modern editions differ only in trivia: most print “everything” as one word where the Folio has “euery thing,” and editors supply the comma after “life.” No word of the sentence is an editorial guess.
context.pull: A consolation speech, not a nature hymn.
